applies_to: revision 1.145 -> candidate 1.147 (joan_wallach_scott: existing person entry; provisional number)

proposed_edges.relationship: Scott recalls first hearing “gender” used in a paper by Davis at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s (2008); her 1986 essay had quoted Davis’s call to study the significance of the sexes
proposed_edges.map_label: Davis and Scott’s first hearing of gender, 1970s–2008
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Scott's own acknowledgement, read in full in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (AHR 113:5, 2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, p. 101): "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90). English renderings are atlas translations from Spanish. Scott sets her own limit on the same page: "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras", and names a second, literary source in her Brown colleagues of the early 1980s. The 1986 quotation of Davis (p. 1054, n. 4) is the existing reading behind edge_1029, which records Davis's contribution to gender history as a field; this edge records Scott's acknowledged personal debt, with the 2008 recollection as new evidence. Not a claim that Davis shared Scott's later theoretical position.

proposed_edges.relationship: Scott draws on psychoanalytic theory, especially the concept of fantasy, to keep gender a critical question: gender as the relation between the normative and the psychic (2008), fantasy as a concept for feminist history (2011), and the productive incommensurability of psychoanalysis and history (2012)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, pp. 108–109): psychoanalytic theory has been useful to her, "no a sus articulaciones conservadoras"; gender is "el estudio de la relación (en torno a la sexualidad) entre lo normativo y lo psíquico, el intento de colectivizar la fantasía". Her 2012 History and Theory abstract (abstract only): psychoanalysis "can force historians to question their certainty about facts, narrative, and cause". Duke's description of The Fantasy of Feminist History (2011; publisher description): she "advocates fantasy as a useful, even necessary, concept for feminist historical analysis". In a 2018 interview she speaks of "a whole psychoanalytic dimension" in Sex and Secularism. Psychoanalysis as a body of theory is the resource; no particular Freud text is claimed. The 2008 reply explains a use of psychoanalysis that "has been useful" to her ("me ha sido útil"); it does not mark a beginning, since the 1986 essay already engaged psychoanalytic theory critically (edge_583, a separate claim about universal sexual antagonism). She still rejects "conservative" psychoanalysis.

proposed_edges.relationship: Scott argues that 1970s psychohistory, shaped by American ego-psychology, assumed a compatibility between psychoanalysis and history that undercut their critical interaction, and proposes a productive incommensurability after de Certeau (2012, in her abstract)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author's abstract only (History and Theory 51:1, 2012, 63–83); the article body is unread. "This was not the case with the movement for psychohistory that began in the 1970s. Then the influence of American ego-psychology on history-writing promoted the idea of compatibility between the two disciplines in ways that undercut the critical possibilities of their interaction." De Certeau supplies "theoretical insight into the uses of incommensurability"; Lyndal Roper's work shows "both its limits and its value". No strand is targeted: the abstract names American ego-psychology, not a particular psychohistorian. Moderate.

proposed_edges.relationship: French feminists caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996), and the parity movement’s attempt to “desymbolize” sex in political representation (Parité!, 2005), as Landes and Dean read them
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated: both books are unread. Landes (APSR 1997, p. 443 read) quotes Scott (p. 173): "competing feminist visions have taken one side or another of the opposition between the abstract individual (which counts women the same as men) and the individual self-defined through sexual difference (which insists on their radical unlikeness)". Dean (H-France Review 2006, read in full): the book "focuses on the challenge parité poses to French universalism" (p. 149); Scott quoted on the strategy of "desymbolization" (p. 54) and on "the human individual as plural, as a type of two" (p. 61) (Dean, p. 150); Dean's query about Muslim women and lesbians (p. 152). Scott herself links French universalism, feminist movements and the politics of the veil as objects of one question about how sexual difference is conceived (Unanswered Questions, Spanish translation, p. 108).

proposed_edges.relationship: The French headscarf ban read as a symptom of republican, colonial and sexual anxieties (The Politics of the Veil, 2007), and a genealogy of secularism contesting the claim that secular societies guarantee gender equality (Sex and Secularism, 2017), in her reviewers’ accounts and her own interview
proposed_edges.map_label: Veil, secularism and the civilizing claim, 2007–2017
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated for the books, which are unread. Laborde (Books & Ideas, 2008, read in full): "Particularly acute are Scott’s analyses of the re-importation of the civilizing mission in post-colonial France"; the ban "acted as a (literally) hysterical diversion" from problems of "class, race and gender". Whitney (Literary Review of Canada, 2018, read in full): the book's "polemical aim" is "to counter the notion that gender equality is somehow inherent in secular societies", working through oppositions such as "west versus Orient, Christianity versus Islam". Scott in a 2018 interview (read in full): post-colonial studies were "critical of the notion that modernity was the end point of the civilizing process"; she sought "a critique or a genealogy that could expose these contradictions". Criticism carried here, not drawn as a separate arrow: Laborde finds the "normative premises and broader political implications" unclear, "a standard limitation of discourse analysis"; O'Grady (Times Higher Education, 2018), a philosopher, objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards: Scott is "anachronistic, ahistorical and oddly absolutist in demanding from 19th-century Europeans moral attitudes that tally with her own". Laborde's objection concerns normative premises and political implications; O'Grady's concerns anachronism. In the 2018 interview Scott names her own difficulty: "how do I write a critique of secularism without rejecting it". A contribution to postcolonial critique of the civilizing narrative, not membership of a school.

proposed_edges.relationship: Laura Lee Downs charges that Scott’s poststructuralist gender severs experience and subjectivity from the agency of the oppressed and treats discourse as “text-writ-large”; Scott replies that Downs misreads theory, which “analyzes how knowledge is produced” (1993)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from women's history, whose experience-and-agency tradition Downs defends. Downs (CSSH 35:2, 1993; p. 414 and the notes shown by the publisher read): Scott's book "has had an especially powerful impact upon historians, for it is through her eyes that many of us have become acquainted with post-structuralist thought"; "There is much to admire"; but it contains "a radical attack on the naïve suppositions of all previous feminist scholarship: a rejection of that ingenuous chain of reasoning which links subjectivity and experience to the hope that oppressed persons, too, might find some agency in history"; notes: "Scott treats discourse as text-writ-large". Scott's reply in the same issue (p. 438 read): "profound misapprehension"; "theory analyzes how knowledge is produced; theory does not produce either real life or practical politics." Distinct from Palmer (edge_920), Valverde (edge_967) and Canning (edge_702).

proposed_edges.relationship: Scott answers Eley and Nield that insisting on class as the best way to analyse inequality forecloses other political categories and other ways of writing critical history (2000, in her abstract)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay).

proposed_edges.relationship: With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder, a call for “critical history” as “theorized history”, against a discipline founded on empiricism, “fetishism of archives” and a gendered dismissal of theory (Theses on Theory and History, 2018)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The collective's own words, read in full (English booklet on the History and Theory site, 2018; cited by thesis). Prologue: theory "displaced by empires of empiricism, fetishism of archives, dictates of discipline, enforcement of orthodoxy, and impotent story-telling"; I.1: "Academic history has never managed to transcend its eighteenth century origins as an empiricist enterprise"; II.1: "An invidious distinction between a feminized philosophy and a masculinized history"; III.1: "Critical history is theorized history"; III.7: "Critical history is a history of the present". Co-authored: credit belongs to all three, and no thesis is assigned to Scott alone. A late intervention in disputes about disciplinary scrutiny, not a resolution of them.

new_sources.title: Carolyn J. Dean, review of Joan Wallach Scott, Parité! Sexual Equality and the Crisis of French Universalism (University of Chicago Press, 2005), H-France Review 6, no. 34 (April 2006): 149–152.
new_sources.citation: Carolyn J. Dean, review of Joan Wallach Scott, Parité! Sexual Equality and the Crisis of French Universalism (University of Chicago Press, 2005), H-France Review 6, no. 34 (April 2006): 149–152.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (publisher PDF, print pages). p. 149: "an elegantly argued and ambitious effort to analyze and historicize the theoretical premises and political practices that shaped the most recent struggle for gender equality in France"; the law passed on 6 June 2000; the book "focuses on the challenge parité poses to French universalism"; Only Paradoxes to Offer (Harvard, 1996) is called "much misunderstood" and described as analysing "feminism’s constitutive contradictions". p. 150: Scott's "often (but not exclusively) symptomatic reading"; the parity strategy of "desymbolization" (Scott p. 54) and "the redefinition of the human individual as plural, as a type of two" (Scott p. 61, as Dean quotes it). p. 151: Agacinski sought to "sex" the political body (Scott p. 115). p. 152: "How, more precisely, might the concept of parité be thought in reference to other multiply 'different' groups such as Muslim women and lesbians?"; "an important contribution not only to the history of French feminism and French republicanism, but to the theory of history." The book is unread; Scott's words are as Dean quotes them.

new_sources.title: Cécile Laborde, “The Politics of the Veil,” Books & Ideas (La Vie des idées), 30 January 2008; review of Joan Wallach Scott, The Politics of the Veil (Princeton University Press, 2007).
new_sources.citation: Cécile Laborde, “The Politics of the Veil,” Books & Ideas (La Vie des idées), 30 January 2008; review of Joan Wallach Scott, The Politics of the Veil (Princeton University Press, 2007).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML, no pagination; date from page metadata). "one of the best Anglo-American critical commentaries" on the headscarf affair and the 2004 law; Scott "takes the discourse of French republicanism … seriously"; the ban "acted as a (literally) hysterical diversion from the profound problems faced by a French society fractured around class, race and gender"; "Particularly acute are Scott’s analyses of the re-importation of the civilizing mission in post-colonial France"; an ideal of "uncovered sexuality" underlay the republican critique of Islam's "covered sexuality"; Scott draws on Baubérot, Balibar, Gaspard, Khosrokhavar and Nordmann. Criticism: "their normative premises and broader political implications remain unclear – a standard limitation of discourse analysis in general"; the counter-discourse of toleration "may turn out to be as problematic" as the republican discourse Scott criticises. Laborde's phrase calling Only Paradoxes Scott's "first major book" is inaccurate and is not reused. The book is unread.

new_sources.title: Susan Whitney, “Is Secularism Really Better for Women?,” Literary Review of Canada, January–February 2018; review of Joan Wallach Scott, Sex and Secularism (Princeton University Press, 2017).
new_sources.citation: Susan Whitney, “Is Secularism Really Better for Women?,” Literary Review of Canada, January–February 2018; review of Joan Wallach Scott, Sex and Secularism (Princeton University Press, 2017).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML, no pagination). Scott's introduction as Whitney quotes it: "this is not a conventional intellectual or social history of the word secularism" but "a set of arguments bound loosely by a periodization related to the emergence of modern western nation-states (from the 18th century on)"; her aim to "open—not to definitively close—a conversation". Whitney: for Scott the book exemplifies Foucault's "history of the present"; its "polemical aim" is "to counter the notion that gender equality is somehow inherent in secular societies"; terms gain meaning through opposites (secularism/religion, man/woman, public/private, west/Orient, Christianity/Islam). Whitney reports Joanne Meyerowitz calling the 1986 article a "foundational text". Verdict: "a challenging, timely, and important book". The book is unread.

new_sources.title: Jane O’Grady, review of Joan Wallach Scott, Sex and Secularism, Times Higher Education, 4 January 2018.
new_sources.citation: Jane O’Grady, review of Joan Wallach Scott, Sex and Secularism, Times Higher Education, 4 January 2018.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML). A philosopher's hostile review: "a useful attempt to redress Western self-congratulation, but it subjects the West to uniquely purist standards"; "Scott claims to espouse Michel Foucault’s “genealogical” approach, yet she is anachronistic, ahistorical and oddly absolutist in demanding from 19th-century Europeans moral attitudes that tally with her own"; O'Grady quotes Scott that modern Western societies were "founded on gender inequality". O'Grady's description of Scott as a sociologist is wrong and is not reused.

new_sources.title: Joan Wallach Scott, “Unanswered Questions,” American Historical Review 113, no. 5 (December 2008): 1422–1430; authorised Spanish translation by Julia Constantino, “Preguntas no respondidas,” Debate Feminista 40 (2009): 100–110.
new_sources.citation: Joan Wallach Scott, “Unanswered Questions,” American Historical Review 113, no. 5 (December 2008): 1422–1430; authorised Spanish translation by Julia Constantino, “Preguntas no respondidas,” Debate Feminista 40 (2009): 100–110.

verification.note: Read for revision 1.147. English original: first two paragraphs only (WebFetch extraction; AHR paywall), including "I want to insist that the term gender is useful only as a question." The Spanish translation, published with the author's permission (Debate Feminista 40, 2009, https://doi.org/10.22201/cieg.2594066xe.2009.40.1441), was read in full; pages below are Debate Feminista pages, and English renderings are the atlas's translations, not Scott's English. p. 101: at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s, "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90); her colleagues at Brown in the early 1980s taught her "que las diferencias sexuales no las establecía la naturaleza, sino que esto se realizaba a través del lenguaje"; "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras". p. 102: gender "trata del planteamiento de preguntas históricas; no es un tratado programático ni metodológico"; she quotes Heidi Tinsman: "lo que conforma una categoría útil para el análisis feminista es un asunto de geopolítica más que una actualización epistemológica" (Tinsman as Scott quotes her; Tinsman's article is unread). p. 108: Meyerowitz wrote that in questioning gender's continued vitality in the 1999 edition Scott moved "en direcciones nuevas"; Scott: "Eso no es totalmente correcto", and she asserts a continuing concern with "cómo se conciben las diferencias entre los sexos", whether the object is French universalism, feminist movements or the politics of the veil (Meyerowitz's article is unread). Also p. 108: in 1999 she worried that gender had "perdido su agudeza crítica"; "me ha sido útil acudir a la teoría psicoanalítica; no a sus articulaciones conservadoras". p. 109: "el género es el estudio de la relación (en torno a la sexualidad) entre lo normativo y lo psíquico, el intento de colectivizar la fantasía"; "es el género el que produce significados para el sexo y la diferencia sexual". pp. 109–110: the question marks removed from the 1986 title perhaps should have stayed.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.147: p. 414 (publisher first-page preview) and the footnote text shown on the Cambridge Core page (note numbers and pages not visible). p. 414: a review essay on Scott's Gender and the Politics of History, which "has had an especially powerful impact upon historians, for it is through her eyes that many of us have become acquainted with post-structuralist thought, particularly the ideas of Jacques Derrida"; "There is much to admire in Scott’s book"; but at its heart "lies a radical attack on the naïve suppositions of all previous feminist scholarship: a rejection of that ingenuous chain of reasoning which links subjectivity and experience to the hope that oppressed persons, too, might find some agency in history". verification.note: Author's abstract read for revision 1.147 (via OpenAlex); the article body is unread. "Psychoanalysis can force historians to question their certainty about facts, narrative, and cause; it introduces disturbing notions about unconscious motivation and the effects of fantasy on the making of history. This was not the case with the movement for psychohistory that began in the 1970s. Then the influence of American ego-psychology on history-writing promoted the idea of compatibility between the two disciplines in ways that undercut the critical possibilities of their interaction." De Certeau supplies "theoretical insight into the uses of incommensurability"; Lyndal Roper's work shows "both its limits and its value".

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML; dated 1 December 2019). Scott treats academic freedom "as an ethical practice in Michel de Certeau’s sense" (Whitaker's words), quoting her: it "defines a distance between what is and what ought to be"; "disciplinary practice is no power-free zone"; Scott ends diagnosing academic freedom "under grave threat from many different directions". Whitaker mentions Scott's service on the AAUP committee on academic freedom (dates not given; not checked). The book is unread.
